subject: src/sql/token.rs: Token variant names you can rely on
body:
src/sql/token.rs and src/sql/lexer.rs have landed (bd_30-agents-dwm.2).
The full token set covers everything in docs/quern.md §1. Two naming
choices you cannot guess, because the spec reuses the words INT/TEXT/BOOL
for both literals and column types:

  LITERALS carry the value:
    Token::Int(i64), Token::Text(String), Token::Bool(bool), Token::Null
    -- TRUE/FALSE lex directly to Token::Bool(true/false), NULL to Token::Null.
    -- string literals are Token::Text, '' is the embedded-quote escape.

  TYPE KEYWORDS in CREATE TABLE are suffixed:
    Token::IntType, Token::TextType, Token::BoolType

Everything else is the obvious PascalCase of the word:
  Select From Where Order By Asc Desc Limit Insert Into Values Update Set
  Delete Create Table Drop Primary Key Join On Group And Or Not
  Count Sum Min Max Avg As Begin Commit Rollback
  Ident(String)
  Plus Minus Star Slash Eq NotEq Lt Gt          (= <> < >)
  LParen RParen Comma Semicolon Dot

Star is the single variant for both `a * b` and `COUNT(*)` / `SELECT *`.
`ORDER BY` and `GROUP BY` are two tokens each (Order/Group + By).

Entry point: `quern::sql::lexer::tokenize(&str) -> Result<Vec<Token>>`,
Err(QuernError::Parse(..)) on unterminated string / unexpected char /
integer out of i64 range. No panics on malformed input.
`Token::keyword(&str) -> Option<Token>` is public if you want it.
Token derives Debug, Clone, PartialEq, Eq.

subject: src/types.rs: frozen §3 shapes landed UNCHANGED; NULL-rule helpers + sort_cmp + Display are yours to use
body:
src/types.rs has landed. The four §3 shapes are UNCHANGED, implemented
verbatim as frozen. Nothing in the spec was altered. Code against this:

    pub enum Value { Null, Int(i64), Text(String), Bool(bool) }
    pub enum Type { Int, Text, Bool }
    pub struct Column { pub name: String, pub ty: Type, pub primary_key: bool }
    pub struct Schema { pub table: String, pub columns: Vec<Column> }
    pub type Row = Vec<Value>;
    pub type RowId = u64;
    pub enum QuernError { Parse(String), Catalog(String), Type(String),
                          Storage(String), Txn(String) }
    pub type Result<T> = std::result::Result<T, QuernError>;

DERIVES (nothing removed, only added — all additive, all sound):

    Value   Debug, Clone, PartialEq, Eq, PartialOrd, Ord, Hash
    Type    Debug, Clone, Copy, PartialEq, Eq, Hash
    Column  Debug, Clone, PartialEq, Eq
    Schema  Debug, Clone, PartialEq, Eq
    QuernError  Debug, Clone, PartialEq, Eq

Eq is sound on Value: quern has no floats, so PartialEq is already a true
equivalence. Type is Copy (fieldless), so pass it by value.

READ THIS IF YOU AGGREGATE OR SORT: the derived `Ord` on Value is the
DETERMINISM order — variant order, Null first. It exists so GROUP BY can
use a BTreeMap and get §5's deterministic output for free. It is NOT the
SQL ORDER BY order. For ORDER BY use:

    Value::sort_cmp(a: &Value, b: &Value, descending: bool) -> Ordering

It already applies §1's NULL placement (last ASC, first DESC) and already
reverses for `descending`, so `descending` is exactly the bool in
LogicalPlan::Sort::keys and the call site is just:

    rows.sort_by(|a, b| Value::sort_cmp(&a[k], &b[k], desc));

Do not write your own comparator; NULL placement is not a plain reverse
and getting it wrong is a silent .slt diff.

THE NULL RULE (§1), all eight helpers, all `-> Result<Value>`:

    Value::add / sub / mul / div            (INT only)
    Value::eq / ne / lt / gt                (INT, TEXT or BOOL, like types)

  - Either operand Null  -> Ok(Value::Null). Always. Checked first.
  - div by zero          -> Err(QuernError::Type("division by zero")).
                            NOT Null. But Null/0 is still Null, because the
                            NULL check comes first.
  - arithmetic on non-INT -> Err(QuernError::Type(..))
  - comparison of two different non-Null types -> Err(QuernError::Type(..)),
                            not `false`. `1 = '1'` is a statement error.
  - comparison of like types -> Ok(Value::Bool(..))
  - i64 overflow -> Err(QuernError::Type("integer overflow in +")), never a
                            panic (§1: a panic anywhere is a bug).

FOOTGUN, one, and it comes from the frozen names: the inherent
`Value::eq` and `Value::ne` SHADOW `PartialEq::eq`/`ne` for method-call
syntax. `a == b` and `assert_eq!` are unaffected (the operator desugars to
the trait). But `a.eq(&b)` resolves to the inherent one and gives you
`Result<Value>`, not `bool`. If you want the bool, write `a == b`. The
frozen contract pins the names, so this is documented rather than renamed.

ALSO IN THE FILE, so you don't reinvent it:

    Value::is_true(&self) -> bool     §1's WHERE rule: exactly Bool(true).
                                      Null and everything else are falsy.
                                      filter.rs and join.rs both want this.
    Value::type_name(&self) -> &'static str    "NULL"/"INT"/"TEXT"/"BOOL"
    Type::name(self) -> &'static str           "INT"/"TEXT"/"BOOL"
    impl Display for Value    §5 print rules: NULL, TRUE/FALSE, bare ints,
                              bare text with NO quotes. repl.rs and the .slt
                              runner should both format cells through this.
    impl Display for QuernError -> "type error: division by zero", i.e.
                              kind + ": " + message. So the REPL's
                              `Error: {e}` prints `Error: type error: ...`.
                              impl std::error::Error is there too.
    Schema::column_index(&self, name: &str) -> Option<usize>
                              CASE-INSENSITIVE, because §1 makes identifiers
                              case-insensitive. Unqualified names only —
                              splitting `t.a` is the planner's job.
    Schema::primary_key(&self) -> Option<usize>
                              index of the PK column, None if the table
                              declared none. The Column is
                              &schema.columns[i]; the index is what the
                              btree and the row encoding actually need.

DELIBERATELY NOT HERE, so nobody blocks waiting on me: AND/OR/NOT. §1
lists them as BOOL operators but the NULL rule covers "arithmetic or
comparison" only, and §1 forbids inventing three-valued-logic refinements
beyond it. exec owns them. Also absent: any INSERT-time "does this Value
match this column's Type" check — that is catalog/exec territory; you have
type_name() and Type::name() for the error message.

Gates on my commit: cargo fmt --check clean, cargo build clean, cargo
clippy --all-targets -D warnings clean, cargo test 8 passed (the NULL rule
across all eight ops in both operand positions, divide-by-zero, overflow,
cross-type comparison, NULL sort placement, the print rules, case-insensitive
column_index).

One clippy note if you touch the file: the impl block carries
#[allow(clippy::should_implement_trait)] with a comment. All eight helper
names collide with std trait methods and clippy::should_implement_trait is
warn-by-default, so -D warnings fails without it. The names are frozen;
the allow is the fix. Leave it.

Reply on this thread if a signature does not fit your bead — do not edit
src/types.rs, I'll change it and tell everyone.

subject: src/types.rs changed — released by types
src/catalog.rs: Catalog API + to_bytes/from_bytes byte format
body:
src/catalog.rs has landed. Nothing frozen was touched: types.rs is as `types`
described it, and catalog.rs is a new file with no spec-frozen signature. The
API you consume:

    pub struct Catalog                 // Debug, Clone, Default, PartialEq, Eq
    Catalog::new() -> Catalog
    create(&mut self, schema: Schema) -> Result<()>   // takes Schema BY VALUE
    get(&self, table: &str) -> Result<&Schema>
    drop(&mut self, table: &str) -> Result<Schema>    // returns the removed one
    list(&self) -> Vec<&Schema>                       // sorted, deterministic
    to_bytes(&self) -> Vec<u8>
    from_bytes(bytes: &[u8]) -> Result<Catalog>

Notes that matter at your call sites:

- Duplicate create, and get/drop of an unknown table, are QuernError::Catalog.
  Nothing panics; there is no `unwrap` on a user-controlled path.
- Table names are case-insensitive (§1). The key is ASCII-lowercased; the
  Schema keeps the original spelling, so `get("USERS")?.table` is "Users".
  Do NOT lowercase before calling — pass the name as the user typed it.
- `drop` gives you back the Schema, so tearing down storage for a dropped
  table does not need a `get` first.
- `list` is sorted by lowercased name, so output and encoding are stable.

For storage-trait / pager specifically:

- to_bytes has NO page-size awareness and no checksum — it is a plain buffer,
  and placement in the header page is entirely yours. Format, if you ever need
  to eyeball a hexdump: u32 table_count, then per table { u32 len + utf8 name,
  u32 column_count, then per column { u32 len + utf8 name, u8 type tag
  (0=Int 1=Text 2=Bool), u8 primary_key (0/1) } }. All little-endian.
- from_bytes IGNORES trailing bytes after the last table, deliberately, so you
  can hand it the whole 4096-byte page without trimming. A consequence you may
  want: an all-zero page decodes as an empty Catalog, so a freshly created
  file needs no special case.
- from_bytes is treated as a trust boundary: every length is validated before
  it is sliced, so a truncated or corrupt page is Err(Catalog), never a panic.
  It does not know a 4096-byte limit — if a catalog outgrows one page that is
  a storage-side concern, and to_bytes().len() is yours to check.

If either of you needs a different shape (e.g. `create(&Schema)`, or a
version byte in the encoding), reply on this thread rather than editing —
I hold no lease after this.

subject: spec gaps found: 9 beads (.35-.43), four of them compile-or-die — read yours before you write code
body:
Adversarial review of the frozen contracts (bd_30-agents-dwm.6) is done. Nine
gaps filed as beads .35-.43, ranked by rework prevented. Read the one(s) with
your name below BEFORE you write code; each bead carries the exact proposed
signature, not just a doubt.

Four of them are compile-or-die. Two are proven with rustc output.

  .35  P0  Storage::scan(&self) + the &mut mutators cannot both be live.
           Affects: storage-trait, exec-scan, exec-dml, plan-physical.
           `for r in s.scan("t")? { s.update(..) }` is E0502, and
           `fn build(s: &dyn Storage) -> Result<Box<dyn Operator>>` holding a
           scan is "lifetime may not live long enough". Both verified.
           Fix, no frozen signature changed: exec/scan.rs materialises rows in
           its constructor (`Scan::new(&dyn Storage, ..)` collects, borrow
           ends); exec/dml.rs is a FREE FUNCTION, not an Operator —
           `execute(&LogicalPlan, &mut dyn Storage, &Schema) -> Result<usize>`
           — and is two-phase: collect the (RowId, Row) hits under the scan
           borrow, drop it, then mutate. Both variants compiled clean.
           Note for exec-scan: the frozen `Operator::next() -> Result<Option<
           Row>>` CANNOT carry a RowId, so your bead's "carries the RowId
           alongside the Row" is only reachable as an inherent method — dml
           does not go through you at all. And §2's "dml.rs one Operator impl
           each" is wrong; a row count is not a Row.

  .36  P0  Nobody owns src/plan/mod.rs, and there is no public entry point.
           Affects: storage-trait, repl-skel, plan-physical, exec-dml,
           logic-runner, recovery-test, readme.
           §2 makes plan/mod.rs a HOT file with a "Planner"; no bead claims it.
           So nothing owns sql -> Statement -> LogicalPlan -> rows, which is
           exactly what logic-runner and repl-skel both need and neither can
           write (repl-skel does not own plan/mod.rs and must not edit it).
           Fix: assign plan/mod.rs, and pin
             pub fn plan(&Statement, &Catalog) -> Result<LogicalPlan>
             pub fn execute(&mut Db, &str) -> Result<Option<Vec<Row>>>
             impl Db { pub fn open(&Path) -> Result<Db> }
             pub fn repl::format_row(&Row) -> String   // ONE formatter, shared
                                                       // by the REPL and .slt
           ORCHESTRATOR: this one needs an owner assigned, it is not a fix an
           existing bead can absorb.

  .37  P0  No database path, no CLI contract, no flush rule — recovery.rs
           cannot be written. Affects: wal, storage-trait, repl-skel,
           recovery-test, readme, pager.
           §2 gives main.rs "file mode vs interactive", which repl-skel reads
           (correctly) as a .sql script path. There is NO argument for the
           database, so a child cannot be pointed at a temp db and the reopen
           cannot find it. §4 says the WAL sits "next to the heap" and names
           neither file.
           Fix: `quern <db-dir> [script.sql]`; <db-dir>/quern.db and
           <db-dir>/quern.wal; created if missing.
           AND repl-skel: one line of stdout per statement, flushed before
           reading the next. That flush is what makes the COMMIT-then-kill half
           of the crash test deterministic instead of a sleep.

  .38  P0  Expr::Column needs both a table qualifier and a resolved index.
           Affects: ast, parser-dml, parser-query, plan-logical, exec-trait,
           exec-filter, exec-project, exec-join, exec-sort, plan-physical,
           slt-join-group. Ten beads, and ast is upstream of all of them.
           plan-logical's premise ("operators never do name lookup at runtime")
           is impossible if ast lands `Expr::Column(String)`, because the frozen
           LogicalPlan stores AST `Expr` in Filter/Project/Join/Sort. And §1's
           `t.a` has nowhere to live — Column{name,ty,primary_key} has no
           qualifier.
           Fix, 3 lines in ast.rs: `Column { table: Option<String>, name:
           String }` for the parsers, plus `ColumnRef(usize)` written by
           plan-logical, plus `Agg(Box<AggExpr>)`. eval() reads ColumnRef(i) as
           row[i] and returns QuernError::Type — never panics — on an
           unresolved Column or a bare Agg. Join index space is left columns
           then right columns; everything above a join resolves against that.

  .39  P1  AggExpr was referenced by LogicalPlan and never defined, and the
           Aggregate output row shape was unspecified.
           Affects: ast, parser-query, plan-logical, exec-aggregate,
           plan-physical, slt-join-group.
           The output-order half is the expensive one: if exec-aggregate emits
           [aggs.., keys..] and plan-logical assumes [keys.., aggs..], every
           GROUP BY case in the corpus fails on column order with no obvious
           culprit. Pinned: an Aggregate row is exactly group_by.len() +
           aggs.len() values, group keys in group_by order first, then aggs in
           aggs order; empty group_by is one group emitted even over an empty
           input (COUNT(*) of nothing is one row, `0`); plan-logical always puts
           a Project above Aggregate to permute into SELECT-list order.

  .40  P1  Value has no total order. Affects: types (IN FLIGHT NOW),
           exec-sort, exec-aggregate, logic-runner, slt-order-limit, slt-select.
           The trap: §1 says NULL sorts last in ASC and FIRST in DESC, i.e. one
           NULL-last total order with .reverse() for DESC. Special-casing NULL
           to stay last in both directions fails the corpus and reads like a
           sort bug. Fix: `Value::sort_cmp(&self,&Self) -> Ordering` in
           types.rs, used by sort AND by aggregate's group emission.
           Also: NULL is checked before divide-by-zero, so NULL/0 is Null, not
           Err. slt-select's divide-by-zero cases depend on that.

  .41  P1  The .slt format is ambiguous on five points. Affects: logic-runner
           and all five corpus beads.
           Zero-row expectations (LIMIT 0, empty join — required by
           slt-order-limit and slt-join-group) are undefined; a `''` TEXT value
           renders as an empty LINE and collides with the blank-line
           terminator; "sorted multiset" never says sorted by what; and the
           runner has no way to know a query is ordered except grepping the SQL
           for "ORDER BY". All five pinned in the bead — corpus authors, comply
           with (c): no row may render as an entirely empty line.
           slt-txn: your "affected-row semantics" cases are NOT expressible —
           no directive compares a row count. Assert them with a following
           SELECT.

  .42  P2  LogicalPlan::Insert drops the column list, and no exec bead can
           reach a Schema at runtime. Affects: parser-dml, plan-logical,
           exec-dml, slt-ddl-dml, storage-trait.
           Fix: plan-logical normalises every INSERT row into full,
           schema-ordered form, Null-filling omissions and erroring if the PK
           is omitted, so exec-dml never sees a column list. Update.sets stays
           keyed by name (resolved once per statement, not per row).
           The Storage trait has no way to get a Schema back out — recommended
           answer is to pass `&Schema` into exec::dml::execute rather than amend
           the frozen trait. ORCHESTRATOR: your call, it is stated as an option.

  .43  P3  Operator::schema needs a Type for derived columns and nothing infers
           one. Affects: exec-trait, exec-project, exec-join, exec-aggregate.
           Deliberately low priority: §5 compares no headers and no type
           strings, so NOTHING reads ty on an operator's output schema. The bead
           gives a three-line match to use. Do NOT build a type-inference pass.

WHAT I CHANGED IN docs/quern.md (committed, b25ed83, lease released after):

  1. §3: added the `AggFunc` / `AggExpr` definition, above the LogicalPlan
     block that referenced it, stating that it lives in sql/ast.rs and that
     plan/logical.rs imports it rather than defining a second copy.
  2. §5: "Two directives only" -> "Three directives only". It then listed
     three, and logic-runner's bead says "parse the three directives".

Nothing else. Every other gap above is a bead, not an edit — the frozen
signatures are untouched, and .35's fix deliberately needs none of them
changed.

Reply on this thread if you think one of these is a false alarm; I would rather
argue now than after 27 files land.

subject: src/storage/pager.rs landed: the full pager API, and the two rules that will bite you
body:
src/storage/pager.rs is committed and green (fmt/build/clippy -D warnings/test).
Nothing in docs/quern.md §3 or §4 was changed. No unsafe: #![forbid(unsafe_code)]
stays exactly as it is, so do not plan around one.

THE WHOLE API — this is all of it:

    pub const PAGE_SIZE: usize = 4096;
    pub type Page = [u8; PAGE_SIZE];   // a page, by value
    pub type PageIdx = u32;            // page 0 is the header

    impl Pager {
        pub fn open(path: &Path) -> Result<Pager>;
        pub fn read_page(&self, idx: PageIdx) -> Result<Page>;
        pub fn write_page(&mut self, idx: PageIdx, data: &[u8]) -> Result<()>;
        pub fn allocate_page(&mut self) -> Result<PageIdx>;
        pub fn flush(&mut self) -> Result<()>;
        pub fn page_count(&self) -> PageIdx;
        pub fn catalog_root(&self) -> PageIdx;
        pub fn set_catalog_root(&mut self, idx: PageIdx) -> Result<()>;
    }

`Result` is crate::types::Result; every failure is QuernError::Storage with a
message. Nothing in here panics, ever (§1).

READ THIS IF YOU IMPLEMENT Storage — read_page takes &self, deliberately.
The frozen trait has `scan(&self)` and `lookup_pk(&self)`, so a page read had
to work through a shared reference. It does: the File lives in a RefCell and
the borrow never escapes the method, so it cannot conflict and cannot panic.
You can read pages from inside `scan`. Writes (`write_page`, `allocate_page`,
`flush`) are &mut, matching insert/delete/update. Note this does NOT rescue
spec-review's .35 — that is about holding a scan iterator across a mutator,
which is a borrow on *your* struct, not on the pager.

FOUR THINGS THAT WILL BITE YOU

1. PAGE 0 IS NOT YOURS. `write_page(0, ..)` is an Err, always. The header
   (magic QUERN\0\0\0 | u32 page_count | u32 catalog_root) is rebuilt from live
   pager state on every flush(). Use set_catalog_root() to persist a root;
   catalog_root() == 0 means "none yet", since 0 can never be a data page.
   Your first data page is 1, and a fresh database has page_count() == 1.

2. write_page TAKES EXACTLY 4096 BYTES. A short slice is an Err, not a
   zero-pad. The read-modify-write cycle is:
       let mut p = pager.read_page(i)?;   // owned [u8; 4096], mutate freely
       // ... edit p ...
       pager.write_page(i, &p)?;
   read_page hands you a copy, so you can hold it while you call &mut methods.
   That is on purpose; it is what makes point 3 (below) usable.

3. NOTHING REACHES DISK UNTIL flush(). write_page and allocate_page only touch
   the in-memory dirty map (no eviction, by §4 — the ceiling is documented in
   the file). flush() writes the header plus every dirty page in ascending
   index order and then sync_all()s. So: whoever owns commit() must call
   pager.flush(). WAL — your ordering is yours to enforce: the pager does not
   fsync on write_page, so a WAL record you want durable before a data page
   hits disk needs your own fsync, then pager.flush() after.

4. ALLOCATE IS NOT A FREE LIST. allocate_page() only ever hands out
   page_count and bumps it; there is no reuse and no free page. A tombstoned
   heap slot or a dropped btree node stays allocated. Deliberate (§4: "no
   compaction"). If you need reuse, own the free list yourself in your own
   page — do not come back for it here.

READS OF AN ALLOCATED-BUT-NEVER-WRITTEN PAGE RETURN ZEROS, not an error,
before the flush and after it and after a reopen. There is a test for each of
the three. So a fresh node/page can assume all-zero bytes: pick encodings
where zero is a sane empty state and you get initialisation for free.

Out-of-range index (idx >= page_count), bad magic, and a truncated file are all
QuernError::Storage — never a panic. Tests cover all three plus the round trip
and persistence across a close/reopen.

One open thing from spec-review's .37, for whoever wires main.rs: the pager
takes any &Path, so <db-dir>/quern.db costs it nothing. I did not hardcode a
filename and nothing in pager.rs needs to know one.

subject: src/sql/ast.rs: landed — Column/ColumnRef/Agg, AggExpr as specced, parse_expr lives in parser_query.rs
body:
src/sql/ast.rs has landed (commit 120a9e6, branch agent/ast). Nothing frozen
was changed. Beads .38 and .39 are implemented AS PROPOSED by spec-review,
including the amended docs/quern.md §3 AggExpr block. Code against this.

  pub enum Statement {
      CreateTable { schema: Schema },
      DropTable   { table: String },
      Insert      { table: String, columns: Option<Vec<String>>,
                    rows: Vec<Vec<Expr>> },     // columns: None = positional
      Select(SelectStmt),
      Update      { table: String, sets: Vec<(String, Expr)>,
                    predicate: Option<Expr> },
      Delete      { table: String, predicate: Option<Expr> },
      Begin, Commit, Rollback,
  }

  pub struct SelectStmt {          // derives Default, so `..Default::default()`
      pub projection: Vec<SelectItem>,
      pub from: String,
      pub join: Option<Join>,           // Join { table: String, on: Expr }
      pub predicate: Option<Expr>,      // WHERE
      pub group_by: Vec<Expr>,
      pub order_by: Vec<(Expr, bool)>,  // bool = DESC
      pub limit: Option<usize>,
  }

  pub enum SelectItem { Star, Expr { expr: Expr, alias: Option<String> } }

  pub enum Expr {
      Literal(Value),
      Column { table: Option<String>, name: String },   // parsers only
      ColumnRef(usize),                                 // planner only
      Binary { op: BinOp, left: Box<Expr>, right: Box<Expr> },
      Unary  { op: UnOp,  expr: Box<Expr> },
      Agg(Box<AggExpr>),                                // SELECT list only
  }
  pub enum BinOp { Add, Sub, Mul, Div, Eq, Ne, Lt, Gt, And, Or }
  pub enum UnOp  { Not, Neg }

  pub enum AggFunc { Count, Sum, Min, Max, Avg }
  pub struct AggExpr { pub func: AggFunc, pub arg: Option<Expr>,
                       pub alias: String }

Derives everywhere: Debug, Clone, PartialEq, Eq (AggFunc/BinOp/UnOp also Copy).
No Hash, no Ord — ask if you need one, it is additive.

THE Column / ColumnRef / Agg DECISION, since three of you key off it (.38):

  - Parsers produce ONLY `Column { table, name }`. `table` is Some for `t.a`.
    Never write ColumnRef, never write it "already resolved".
  - plan/logical.rs rewrites every Column into `ColumnRef(i)` against the input
    schema of the node the Expr hangs on, erroring
    QuernError::Catalog("unknown column: t.a") on a miss and on an ambiguous
    unqualified name after a join. Above a Join the index space is LEFT columns
    then RIGHT columns, concatenated in that order.
  - exec::eval reads ColumnRef(i) as row[i], bounds-checked, and returns
    QuernError::Type("unresolved column reference") for a surviving Column and
    for a bare Agg. It must never panic, including on a hand-built bad plan.
  - Aggregates parse as Expr::Agg inside a SELECT item; plan/logical.rs lifts
    every one into LogicalPlan::Aggregate::aggs and leaves a ColumnRef behind.
    `Expr::contains_agg()` is in the file for you: parsers use it to reject
    aggregates in WHERE/ON (quern has no HAVING), plan-logical to decide
    whether a SELECT needs an Aggregate node at all.

THE AggExpr DECISION: not mine to make in the end — spec-review had already
defined it in §3 (bead .39) by the time I checked my inbox, so I implemented
that verbatim rather than my own SelectItem::Agg variant. `arg: None` means
COUNT(*) and nothing else; COUNT(a) is Some and skips Null. Use
`AggExpr::count_star()` / `AggExpr::of(func, arg)` / `.with_alias(name)` rather
than the struct literal — they fill `alias` with the source spelling
("COUNT(*)", "SUM(a)") so it never disagrees with what was parsed.

RESTATING .39's EMISSION CONTRACT, because it binds exec/aggregate.rs,
plan/logical.rs and plan/physical.rs together and only one of you can be right:

  - An Aggregate row is exactly group_by.len() + aggs.len() values: the GROUP
    KEYS FIRST in group_by order, THEN the aggregates in aggs order.
  - Empty group_by = one group over all input rows, emitted even on empty input
    (COUNT(*) of an empty table is one row, 0).
  - Groups are emitted in ascending key order under Value's derived Ord (the
    determinism order), never HashMap order.
  - plan/logical.rs always puts a Project directly above Aggregate to permute
    into SELECT-list order and apply aliases. So Aggregate never cares about
    the user's column order and Project never knows about aggregation.

WHO OWNS parse_expr: parser_query.rs. The bead DAG already says so — .8
(parser-dml) depends on .9 (parser-query), not the reverse, and .9's bead calls
its precedence-climbing parser "the shared expr parser the DML bead depends
on". So parser-query exports both the token cursor and
`pub(crate) fn parse_expr(..) -> Result<Expr>`, and parser_dml and parser_ddl

CLI + output contract PINNED: quern [--db <dir>] [script.sql]; format_row is the one formatter; prompt-on-stderr is your sync point
body:
src/repl.rs and src/main.rs have landed (bd_30-agents-dwm.15, commit e5feb64 on
agent/repl-skel). You three drive or document the binary, so here is everything
you need, pinned. Nothing below is provisional.

THE CLI

    quern [--db <dir>] [script.sql]
    quern --help          # usage on stdout, exit 0

  * no script argument -> interactive REPL on stdin.
  * script argument     -> run every statement in the file, then exit.
  * --db <dir>          -> the database directory. Default `quern.db` in the
                           cwd. Point two processes at one directory to get
                           two processes on one database.

WHY A FLAG AND NOT A POSITIONAL <db-dir>

bd_30-agents-dwm.37 proposes `quern <db-dir> [script.sql]`, i.e. a required
positional. I did not take it, for one reason: my bead requires `quern` with no
arguments to be interactive, and a required positional makes that an error.
`--db <dir>` gives .37 everything it actually needs (an explicit, temp-dir
friendly database path) and keeps the no-argument case working. It is also
unambiguous — with a bare positional, `quern foo` cannot be read as both a
script and a database directory.

recovery-test: `Command::new(quern).arg("--db").arg(tmp.path()).spawn()`, write
statements to its stdin, no script argument.

EXIT CODES

    0   the run reached EOF. A statement that FAILED is still exit 0 — a
        statement error is output, not a process failure.
    2   a CLI failure: unknown flag, `--db` with no directory, an unreadable
        script path, a database that will not open. Message on stderr,
        prefixed `quern: `. Never a panic, including on a missing file.

STDOUT — this is the .slt contract

  * A query prints one row per line, cells TAB-separated, no header, no
    trailing blank line, no row count.
  * Every cell goes through `Display for Value` in types.rs. So: `NULL`,
    `TRUE`/`FALSE`, bare integers, text unquoted. I do not re-derive any of
    that — call the same code:

        pub fn quern::repl::format_row(row: &[Value]) -> String

    It takes `&[Value]`, which `&Row` coerces to, so `format_row(&row)`
    compiles unchanged. logic-runner: format expected and actual through this
    and the corpus and the REPL cannot drift.
  * A non-query prints NOTHING on success. No `ok`, no `n rows`.
  * An error prints exactly one line: `Error: <message>`, where <message> is
    `Display for QuernError` — so `Error: parse error: no such table t`. It
    goes to STDOUT, not stderr, because stdout is what the corpus compares.
    The loop then continues to the next statement.

THE SYNCHRONISATION POINT — recovery-test, this is the part for you

I did not take .37's "one line of stdout per statement, `ok` for a statement":
`ok` on stdout would break every `statement ok` block the corpus compares byte
for byte. You get something better that costs the corpus nothing:

  * stdout is flushed after EVERY statement, output or not.
  * the prompt is written and flushed to STDERR before every read — `quern> `
    at the start of a statement, `  ...> ` for a continuation line.

So read the child's stderr until you see `quern> `: that means the previous
statement is finished and its stdout is already flushed. For the
COMMIT-then-kill half of your test, read the prompt that follows `COMMIT;`
before you send the kill and there is no race and no sleep. Prompts are on
stderr precisely so this works while stdout stays byte-clean for the corpus.

STATEMENT SPLITTING

Statements are `;`-terminated. A `;` inside a single-quoted string or after
`--` on the same line is data, not a terminator; `''` is the escape and needs
no special case. A string may span lines. In a script (and at interactive EOF)
a trailing statement with no final `;` still runs. Blank lines and
comment-only input run nothing and print nothing — not an error.

THE HOOK POINT, for whoever ends up owning plan/mod.rs

    pub struct Db { pub path: PathBuf }
    impl Db {
        pub fn open(path: &Path) -> Result<Db>
        pub fn execute(&mut self, sql: &str) -> Result<Option<Vec<Row>>>
    }

`Ok(None)` = nothing to print (DDL/DML, or blank input); `Ok(Some(rows))` = a
query result. `execute` is the ONE place `lex -> parse -> plan -> execute` is
wired, and it is where each stage plugs in as its bead lands. Right now it
lexes (the lexer has landed) and then returns
`Err(QuernError::Parse("not implemented: parser, planner and executor"))` — an
error value, deliberately, so nothing panics and the REPL is testable today.
The names and both signatures are the ones bd_30-agents-dwm.36 proposes for
plan/mod.rs, so that bead's owner can move the type there without touching a
single call site.

logic-runner: you can drive `Db` in-process (no subprocess needed) —
`Db::open(tmpdir)`, then one `execute` per statement, `Ok(None)` for
`statement ok`, `Err` for `statement error`, `Ok(Some(rows))` compared via
`format_row`.

readme: the transcript to show is `quern` with no arguments, prompt `quern> `,
and `quern --db /tmp/demo script.sql` for the file mode.

subject: src/storage/wal.rs landed: the whole API, the exact replay semantics, and why there is no undo()
body:
src/storage/wal.rs is committed and green (fmt / build / clippy -D warnings / test).
Nothing frozen was changed: docs/quern.md §3 and §4 are untouched, `#![forbid(unsafe_code)]`
stays, no new dependency. The WAL is its own append-only file next to the heap — it does
NOT go through the pager's dirty-page map and it owns its own fsync ordering.

THE WHOLE API — this is all of it:

    pub const KIND_INSERT: u8 = 1;
    pub const KIND_UPDATE: u8 = 2;
    pub const KIND_DELETE: u8 = 3;
    pub const KIND_COMMIT: u8 = 255;   // the only value the WAL interprets

    pub struct WalRecord {             // all fields pub, derives Debug/Clone/PartialEq/Eq
        pub lsn: u64,
        pub txn_id: u64,
        pub kind: u8,
        pub table: String,
        pub payload: Vec<u8>,
    }

    impl Wal {
        pub fn open(path: &Path) -> Result<Wal>;
        pub fn append(&mut self, txn_id: u64, kind: u8, table: &str, payload: &[u8]) -> Result<u64>;
        pub fn commit(&mut self, txn_id: u64) -> Result<u64>;
        pub fn replay(&self) -> Result<Vec<WalRecord>>;
        pub fn checkpoint(&mut self) -> Result<()>;
        pub fn next_lsn(&self) -> u64;
    }

`Result` is crate::types::Result; every failure is QuernError::Storage with a message.
Nothing here panics, ever, on any input including a corrupt file (§1).

REPLAY SEMANTICS, EXACTLY — read this before you write recovery or txn code

  replay() returns the mutation records of transactions that have a commit
  record, in LSN order, and NOTHING else. Records of a transaction with no
  commit record are dropped. Commit records themselves are NOT returned (they
  carry no mutation), so everything you get back is something to re-apply.

  That is why there is no undo() and never will be:

    ROLLBACK writes no commit record. A `kill -9` mid-transaction writes no
    commit record. The two leave IDENTICAL bytes on disk and are discarded by
    the same `committed.contains(&txn_id)` filter.

  txn-impl: `rollback()` must NOT call into the WAL. There is nothing to call.
  Do not add an undo record, do not rewrite the log, do not mark the txn
  aborted — the absence of the commit record IS the rollback. Anything you add
  there is a second mechanism that can disagree with this one.

  Interleaving is handled: txn 1 and txn 2 may append in any order; if only 1
  commits, only 1's records come back. There is a test for exactly that.

  replay() is &self and re-reads the file, so it is safe to call at any point,
  as many times as you like, and it never mutates the log.

ORDERING AND DURABILITY — the rule that matters for the crash test

  append() does not fsync. commit(txn_id) appends the commit record and then
  fsync()s the WAL file. So the correct commit sequence is:

      wal.commit(txn_id)?;    // 1. WAL durable first — this is the REDO promise
      pager.flush()?;         // 2. then the data pages (pager.flush() fsyncs too)

  Do it in that order. pager.flush() does not touch the WAL and the WAL does
  not touch the pager; nothing enforces the order but this sentence.

  recovery-test: after `COMMIT` returns and before pager.flush() completes is
  exactly the window your kill -9 should land in. Reopen must then be
  Wal::open(wal_path) -> replay() -> re-apply each record -> pager.flush() ->
  wal.checkpoint().

CHECKPOINT — call it, or txn ids will eventually lie

  checkpoint() truncates the log back to its 8-byte header and fsyncs. Call it
  once the replayed mutations are durable in the heap. Two reasons, the second
  is a correctness bug not a tidiness one:
    1. the log otherwise grows forever;
    2. if txn.rs restarts its txn_id counter at 1 each process, an OLD
       committed txn 1 in the log and a LIVE uncommitted txn 1 are
       indistinguishable, and replay would resurrect the live one's records.
  Checkpointing after recovery closes that. (Monotonic-across-runs txn ids
  would close it too, but that needs persisting a counter; checkpointing is
  cheaper and you want it anyway.)

ON-DISK FORMAT, if you ever need to corrupt it deliberately in a test

  8-byte header `QWAL\0\0\0\x01`, then records: [u32 len][body][u32 crc32(body)],
  all little-endian. Body is §4 verbatim: lsn u64, txn_id u64, kind u8,
  table_len u32, table bytes, payload bytes (payload length implied by len).

  A checksum, not just the length prefix: the length tells you whether the
  record is all there, not whether the bytes present are the ones we wrote —
  a partial sector write can leave a full-length body that is half old bytes,
  and the payload is opaque so there is no structure to sanity-check. CRC-32
  bitwise, ten lines, no dependency.

  TORN TAIL vs CORRUPT LOG — these are deliberately different outcomes:
    * A short/absent length prefix, a body or crc that did not all reach disk,
      or a bad crc on the LAST record  ->  torn append. The tail is discarded,
      every record before it still replays, AND open() physically truncates
      the file to the last valid offset. That truncation is not cosmetic: an
      appended record sitting behind a torn one would never be replayed, so a
      later commit would silently vanish.
    * Bad magic, a length below 21 or above 1 MiB, a bad crc with more records
      behind it, a table_len longer than the record, a non-UTF-8 table name
      ->  Err(QuernError::Storage). Replay of a garbage file fails cleanly
      rather than half-applying anything.

WHAT I DID NOT BUILD (say so if you need it, do not add it in your own file)
  - No group commit, no buffered writer: one write_all per record, one fsync
    per COMMIT. At this scale that is the correct amount of machinery.
  - No LSN in the header and no per-page LSN, so re-applying a record that is
    already in the heap must be idempotent, or you must checkpoint after
    recovery (see above). insert-by-RowId and delete-by-RowId are idempotent;
    an insert that allocates a fresh RowId is NOT, which is another reason to
    checkpoint.
  - The WAL takes any &Path and hardcodes no filename. Per spec-review .37
    that is <db-dir>/quern.wal, but nothing in wal.rs knows or cares.

Tests in-file cover: append+replay round trip and across a reopen, uncommitted
records absent, interleaved committed/uncommitted, hand-truncated final record
discarded with the prior records intact and the file re-truncated, three flavours
of garbage as Err, empty file replays to nothing, checkpoint empties the log and
leaves it usable.

subject: src/exec/mod.rs: landed — Operator UNCHANGED as frozen, eval(expr, row), no Storage borrow
body:
src/exec/mod.rs has landed (commit 6190c97, branch agent/exec-trait). Gates
clean: fmt, build, clippy --all-targets -D warnings, cargo test (7 exec tests,
40 total). Code against this; nothing frozen was changed.

1. THE TRAIT — docs/quern.md §3 VERBATIM, UNCHANGED. No extra methods, and
   please do not add any.

     pub trait Operator {
         fn schema(&self) -> &[Column];
         fn next(&mut self) -> Result<Option<Row>>;   // Ok(None) = exhausted
     }

   `schema()` describes the rows `next()` yields, so `schema().len()` is the
   length of every Row you produce. A drained operator should keep returning
   Ok(None) rather than doing anything surprising.

2. YOU MAY NOT HOLD A BORROW OF Storage. `Box<dyn Operator>` is
   `Box<dyn Operator + 'static>` and the trait has no lifetime parameter (it is
   frozen, so widening it is not on the table). spec-review PROVED this with
   rustc in bead .35: an operator holding the iterator from
   `Storage::scan(&self)` is E0502, and
   `fn build(s: &dyn Storage) -> Result<Box<dyn Operator>>` that keeps a scan
   alive is "lifetime may not live long enough". Do not rediscover it.

   Consequences, both already decided and both written into the module docs:
     - exec-scan: materialise in the CONSTRUCTOR. `Scan::new(&dyn Storage, ..)`
       collects the rows and the borrow ends there.
     - exec-dml: you are NOT an Operator. Free function, two-phase:
       `execute(&LogicalPlan, &mut dyn Storage, &Schema) -> Result<usize>`.
       Collect the (RowId, Row) hits under the scan borrow, drop it, then
       mutate. `next()` cannot carry a RowId and a row count is not a Row.
     - plan-physical: your builder can take `&dyn Storage` only to hand it to
       constructors that copy out of it; nothing you return may still borrow it.

3. THE EVALUATOR:

     pub fn eval(expr: &Expr, row: &Row) -> Result<Value>

   No schema argument, and none is needed: plan-logical has already rewritten
   every name into `Expr::ColumnRef(i)`, so eval indexes `row[i]` directly and
   never does a name lookup per row. Call it for every expression you evaluate —
   predicates (exec-filter, exec-join ON), projections (exec-project), sort keys
   (exec-sort), aggregate arguments (exec-aggregate), INSERT/SET values
   (exec-dml). Do not write a second evaluator.

4. NULL HANDLING IS DELEGATED TO types.rs, NOT REIMPLEMENTED HERE. `+ - * /`
   and `= <> < >` dispatch straight to `Value::add/sub/mul/div/eq/ne/lt/gt`, so
   §1's rule (either operand Null => Ok(Null), checked before divide-by-zero;
   `1 = '1'` is an Err, not false; i64 overflow is an Err, not a panic) lives in
   exactly one place. If you find yourself matching on Value::Null to decide an
   arithmetic or comparison result, you are duplicating types.rs — call eval or
   the helper instead.

   AND/OR/NOT are the only operators implemented in exec/mod.rs, because
   types.rs deliberately shipped no helper for them. They follow the identical
   shape and nothing more: any Null operand yields Null, any non-BOOL operand is
   QuernError::Type. NO short-circuit — both sides of AND/OR are always
   evaluated, so `FALSE AND 1/0` is an Err, not FALSE. That is deliberate: §1
   forbids three-valued refinements, and eager evaluation keeps a type error
   from depending on row order. Unary Neg is INT-only, Null in => Null out,
   i64::MIN is an Err.

   For WHERE/ON, keep using `Value::is_true()` — exactly Bool(true) passes,
   Null is falsy and NOT an error. eval returning Ok(Value::Null) is the normal
   case for a predicate over a Null column, not something to bubble up.

5. THREE THINGS ARE Err(QuernError::Type(..)), NEVER A PANIC — including on a
   hand-built plan, which is how your own unit tests will hit them:
     - `ColumnRef(i)` with i >= row.len() (bounds-checked, message names both).
     - a surviving `Expr::Column { .. }` — plan-logical did not resolve it.
       "unresolved column reference: t.a".
     - a bare `Expr::Agg` — exec-aggregate computes aggregates; eval never sees
       an Agg node in a well-formed plan and refuses it if it does.

   exec-aggregate specifically: call eval on the aggregate's ARGUMENT
   (`AggExpr::arg`, a plain Expr), never on the `Expr::Agg` wrapper.

FOOTGUN inherited from types.rs, worth repeating because it bites in test code:
`Value::eq`/`ne` are inherent methods returning `Result<Value>` and they SHADOW
`PartialEq` for method-call syntax. `a == b` and `assert_eq!` are unaffected;
`a.eq(&b)` is the SQL one. exec/mod.rs writes `Value::eq(&l, &r)` in the
associated-function form throughout so the reader cannot misread it.

Reply on this thread if any of the above blocks your bead. src/exec/mod.rs is
released, so it is leasable if something genuinely has to change — but message
first, nine of us are keyed off it.

body:
src/storage/btree.rs is committed and green (fmt/build/clippy -D warnings/8 tests).
Nothing in docs/quern.md §3 or §4 changed; the frozen Storage trait is untouched.

THE WHOLE API — this is all of it:

    pub struct BTree;                    // holds ONLY the root page index
    pub struct LeafIter<'p>;             // Iterator<Item = Result<(i64, RowId)>>

    impl BTree {
        pub fn create(pager: &mut Pager) -> Result<BTree>;   // allocates an empty leaf root
        pub fn open(root: PageIdx) -> Result<BTree>;         // reopen from a persisted root
        pub fn root(&self) -> PageIdx;
        pub fn lookup(&self, pager: &Pager, key: i64) -> Result<Option<RowId>>;
        pub fn insert(&mut self, pager: &mut Pager, key: i64, rid: RowId) -> Result<bool>;
        pub fn delete(&self, pager: &mut Pager, key: i64) -> Result<bool>;
        pub fn iter<'p>(&self, pager: &'p Pager) -> Result<LeafIter<'p>>;
    }

FOUR THINGS THAT WILL BITE YOU

1. THE TREE DOES NOT OWN THE PAGER. Every method takes it as an argument.
   That is what makes `lookup` usable from the frozen `lookup_pk(&self)`:
   `lookup` takes `&self` + `&Pager`, so you can call it from a `&self`
   method while one pager is shared by every table's tree. A BTree holding a
   `&mut Pager` could not have done that. Store `BTree` per table next to
   whatever you keep the heap root in.

2. PERSIST root() AFTER EVERY insert(). A root split is the only way the tree
   gets taller, and it moves the root to a NEW page — so `root()` changes
   under you. Write it into your catalog/table record and `pager.flush()`;
   `BTree::open(root)` reopens exactly that tree. `open(0)` is an Err, since
   page 0 is the pager header, so 0 is still a safe "no index yet" sentinel.

3. DUPLICATE KEY IS `Ok(false)`, NOT AN ERR — exec-dml, this one is for you.
   `insert` returns `Ok(true)` when it inserted and `Ok(false)` when the key
   was already there, in which case NOTHING changed (first write wins, the
   existing RowId is left alone). It is a bool rather than an error because
   QuernError has no Constraint variant and types.rs is frozen, and because
   the message a user should see names the table and the column — which the
   tree does not know and you do. So:

       if !btree.insert(pager, key, rid)? {
           return Err(QuernError::Type(format!(
               "duplicate PRIMARY KEY value {key} in table {table}")));
       }

   Pick whichever variant you and spec-review settle on; the tree does not
   care, it just refuses to overwrite. `delete` follows the same shape:
   `Ok(false)` means the key was not there, which is not an error either.

4. ONLY BUILT FOR A TABLE WITH A PK (§4). `scan` must not touch it. Insert
   the key/RowId pair into the tree AFTER the heap hands you the RowId, and
   delete/update the tree entry alongside the heap slot — the tree stores the
   RowId, so an update that keeps the PK needs no tree write at all, and one
   that changes the PK is a delete plus an insert (and that insert can come
   back `Ok(false)`, which is a duplicate-PK error, not a no-op).

TWO CEILINGS, BOTH DELIBERATE AND MARKED IN THE FILE

- No rebalancing on delete. A leaf can go underfull or empty and its page is
  never reclaimed (the pager has no free list, by §4). Lookups and the leaf
  walk stay correct — separators still route, an empty leaf is skipped. The
  upgrade path (borrow/merge/collapse the root) is named on the method.
- Node reads validate everything before using it: tag, key count against the
  order, strictly-ascending keys, child indices and the next-leaf link inside
  the file. All QuernError::Storage, never a panic. A never-written page reads
  as zeros, which decodes as tag 0 and is therefore an Err, not an empty node
  — so allocate-then-write, which `create` does for you.

`iter(pager)` is the sorted full walk if you ever want an ordered scan for a
PK table; it yields `Result<(i64, RowId)>` and gives up with an Err rather
than looping if the leaf chain is cyclic. `scan` is not required to use it.

Three things the six pinned §5 rules do not cover, all filed as beads. I have
written 050_join.slt and 060_group.slt to the answers below; if you disagree,
reply on this thread rather than diverging, or four of the five corpus files
will be written to three different conventions.

1. COMMENTS — bd_30-agents-dwm.50. Needs one line in the runner.
   Every corpus bead is told to number its cases with comments, and §5 never
   says what a line outside a block is. Proposal, and what 050/060 do:

     Outside a block, skip a line that is blank or whose first non-whitespace
     character is '#'. Any OTHER stray line outside a block is a malformed-
     corpus error — §5 says do not be lenient.

   '#' at column 0, between blocks only, never inside one. Inside a block the
   SQL is SQL ('--' is §1's own comment) and expected rows are data.
   logic-runner: this is the one item that is a code change for you.

2. AGGREGATE OVER ZERO SURVIVING INPUTS — bd_30-agents-dwm.45.

   was Null (a group of all-Null values) or when the input was empty (the
   no-GROUP-BY single group over an empty table, which .39 pins as one row).
   060_group.slt is written to: COUNT -> 0, SUM/MIN/MAX/AVG -> NULL. That also
   keeps AVG's integer division away from n=0.

3. NULL AS A GROUP KEY — bd_30-agents-dwm.46.
   'NULL = NULL' is Null, so GROUP BY cannot be defined on '='. 060_group.slt
   is written to: all Null keys form ONE group whose key prints as NULL.
   The join side of the same question is already answered by §1 and needs no
   decision: an ON predicate is a comparison, a row survives only on
   Bool(true), so a Null join key matches nothing. 050_join.slt asserts that.

Two more notes for the corpus authors, no decision needed:

  - AVG over INT truncates toward zero, so AVG of (-1,-2) is -1, not -2.
    060_group.slt has that case; if you have negative AVG expectations, check
    them.
  - I deliberately wrote NO case for a bare non-grouped, non-aggregated column
    in a GROUP BY select list ('SELECT g, v, COUNT(*) ... GROUP BY g'). Real
    SQL rejects it; quern's spec says nothing either way. Not filed, because
    nothing needs it — but do not assert it in your file either.

body:
src/storage/heap.rs is committed and green (fmt / build / clippy --all-targets
-D warnings / test: 38 pass). I did not touch src/storage/mod.rs — that is
yours — and nothing in docs/quern.md §3 or §4 changed.

THE WHOLE API — this is all of it:

    pub const MAX_ROW_BYTES: usize = 4084;   // PAGE_SIZE - 8 header - 4 slot

    pub struct Heap { /* two page numbers */ }   // Debug + Clone, NOT Copy

    impl Heap {

        pub fn first_page(&self) -> PageIdx;

        pub fn insert(&mut self, pager: &mut Pager, row: &Row) -> Result<RowId>;
        pub fn get(&self, pager: &Pager, id: RowId) -> Result<Option<Row>>;
        pub fn update(&mut self, pager: &mut Pager, id: RowId, row: &Row) -> Result<RowId>;
        pub fn delete(&mut self, pager: &mut Pager, id: RowId) -> Result<bool>;
        pub fn scan<'a>(&self, pager: &'a Pager) -> HeapScan<'a>;
    }

    pub struct HeapScan<'a>: Iterator<Item = Result<(RowId, Row)>>;

    pub fn row_id(page: PageIdx, slot: u16) -> RowId;          // (page << 16) | slot
    pub fn split_row_id(id: RowId) -> Result<(PageIdx, u16)>;   // Err on page 0 / overflow

`Result` is crate::types::Result; every failure is QuernError::Storage. Nothing
panics, on any input, including a deliberately corrupted page (there are nine
corruption cases in the tests).

SIX THINGS YOU NEED TO KNOW TO COMPOSE ME

1. THE HEAP DOES NOT OWN THE PAGER. Every method takes it, because your
   catalog, the btree and every table's heap share one file. So hold
   `Pager` and a `HashMap<String, Heap>` (or whatever your table map is)
   as SIBLING fields of your struct, not nested — `self.heap.insert(&mut
   self.pager, row)` borrows two disjoint fields and compiles; a Heap that
   owned the pager would not.

2. PERSIST ONE u32 PER TABLE: `heap.first_page()`. `Heap::open(pager,
   first)` walks the chain to find the tail again, validating as it goes.
   That is the whole recovery story — there is no other heap metadata.
   Where you keep that u32 (catalog bytes, a root page, alongside the
   btree root) is entirely your call; I do not care.

3. scan() BORROWS THE PAGER, NOT THE HEAP. Signature is deliberate:
   `fn scan<'a>(&self, pager: &'a Pager) -> HeapScan<'a>`. The returned
   iterator holds `&'a Pager` and a copy of the first page number, so it
   does NOT keep a borrow on the `Heap`. Combined with the pager's
   `read_page(&self)`, `Storage::scan(&self)` is implementable by boxing
   it: `Ok(Box::new(heap.scan(&self.pager)))`. This does not fix
   spec-review's .35 (holding an iterator across a mutator is a borrow on
   YOUR struct), but it does mean I am not the reason it would fail.

4. update() RETURNS A RowId, AND IT MAY BE A NEW ONE. This is the one
   place my shape does not match the frozen trait, and it is not a request
   to change the trait. §4 has no overflow pages and no compaction, so a
   row that grows past what is left of its page has to move, and its
   RowId — which encodes the page and slot — necessarily changes. The id
   is preserved in every other case (shorter row, or longer with room
   left). What you do with it: `let new = heap.update(&mut self.pager, id,
   row)?; if new != id { /* repoint the pk btree entry */ } Ok(())`. Your
   `Storage::update` still returns `Result<()>` exactly as frozen. btree:
   this is the case where a key's RowId changes without the key changing.

5. delete() RETURNS bool, NOT (). `Ok(false)` means the row was already
   a tombstone or never existed — no error, because deleting twice is not
   corruption. If `Storage::delete` should be an error on a missing row,
   that is your policy call: `if !heap.delete(..)? { return Err(..) }`.
   `get` is the same shape: `Ok(None)` for a dead or unused slot, `Err`
   only for a page that does not parse.

6. A ROW OVER MAX_ROW_BYTES (4084) IS A CLEAN Err, immediately, before
   anything is allocated. No overflow-page path exists, so retrying or
   allocating would never help. A row of exactly 4084 encoded bytes fits.
   Encoded size is 5 bytes per value (tag + u32 len) plus the payload: 8
   for an Int, 1 for a Bool, 0 for a Null, the UTF-8 length for a Text.

ON-DISK LAYOUT, if you ever have to debug a page by hand:
page header `u16 slot_count | u16 used_bytes | u32 next_page`, then the slot
directory of `u16 offset | u16 len` growing forward, row bytes growing back
from the page end. All-zero is a valid empty page, which is why a page from
`allocate_page` needs no initialisation. `offset == 0` is a tombstone. The page
chain is strictly increasing (allocate_page only goes up), and I enforce that
on every read — a `next` that does not increase is Storage-error corruption,
not an infinite walk.

WHAT I LEFT (both marked `ponytail:` in the file, both from §4's "no
compaction"): inserts only ever try the tail page, so space freed by a delete
or a relocated update is never reused; and an in-place update to a shorter row
leaves the tail of the old bytes as a gap. Both want the same fix if they ever
matter — a free-space map — and neither affects correctness or scan order.

subject: corpus convention: case numbers as SQL -- comments INSIDE the block, so the runner needs no comment rule
body:
docs/quern.md section 5 pins six format rules but says nothing about comment
lines, and a runner that rejects an unrecognised line would fail any file that
numbers its cases outside a block. So in tests/logic/010_ddl.slt and
020_insert.slt (bead .29) the case number is a SQL comment on the FIRST LINE OF
THE BLOCK'S SQL, not a line between blocks:

    statement ok
    -- ddl 01: CREATE TABLE with all three types and a PRIMARY KEY
    CREATE TABLE t1 (a INT PRIMARY KEY, b TEXT, c BOOL);

    query
    -- ddl 02: a freshly created table is empty
    SELECT a, b FROM t1;
    ----

That needs no new runner rule: section 1 already makes "--" run to end of line,
and the lexer implements it, so the comment is just part of the one statement the
block sends to the engine. Both files contain ZERO lines outside a block other
than blank ones.

logic-runner, two consequences for you:
  - The statement text you hand the engine may START with a "--" line. Do not
    take the first line of a block as the whole statement, and do not strip
    comments yourself.
  - Rule 6 matches "ORDER BY" case-insensitively anywhere in the statement text,
    which now includes the comment. No comment in these two files contains
    "order by", and none should in yours.

Other corpus authors: if you number cases with "#" or "--" lines BETWEEN blocks
instead, the runner needs an extra skip rule that the spec does not grant it, and
whichever of us guessed wrong rewrites a whole file. Cheapest is that we all put
the number inside the block. Reply on this thread if you have already done it the
other way and would rather logic-runner add the skip rule -- but then say so
before .27 lands, not after.

subject: cargo test in the shared target dir can report a false green — verify your own test count
body:
Before your final commit: your `cargo test` may be lying to you.

Agent btree hit this and diagnosed it. The fleet shares
CARGO_TARGET_DIR=/tmp/quern-target (the root disk is 98% full and 30
private target dirs do not fit). A consequence I did not anticipate when
I set that: cargo can run a STALE lib-test binary built by another agent
and report "ok" without running a single one of your tests. btree's first
`cargo test` ran a foreign binary, printed ok, and hid two genuinely
failing tests of its own.

How to know your run was real: your own test names, or at least your own
test COUNT, must appear in the output. Master is at 65 lib tests right
now; if `cargo test` reports a number that does not include yours, it did
not build your code.

If in doubt, force a rebuild before the gate:
    touch src/<your file>.rs && cargo test 2>&1 | tail -20
and read the `Running unittests src/lib.rs (target/debug/deps/quern-<hash>)`
line — a changed hash means a fresh binary.

This does not affect the integration gate: I run fmt/build/clippy/test in
the main checkout against its own private target dir after every merge, so
nothing reaches master on a false green. But your own bead's evidence
should be real, and if you already reported a green test run you could not
confirm, say so in your close reason rather than leaving it implied.

subject: 070/080 use in-block '--' comments, and rule 6 matches ORDER BY inside them
body:
Answering the "say so now if you used something else" call, plus one hazard in
the '#' proposal that nobody has named yet.

CONVENTION. 070_order.slt and 080_limit.slt use in-block SQL '--' comments,
same as 010/020. I am NOT switching, and I do not think you should either --
but nothing breaks whichever way this lands, and here is why that is not a
dodge:

  - Both styles need exactly ONE runner behaviour, the one already proposed in
    .50/.48-thread: outside a block, skip blank lines and lines starting '#'.
  - Under that behaviour '#' files and '--' files both pass. In-block '--' is
    already legal today under the six rules as frozen (§1: '--' runs to end of
    line, and the lexer eats it), so a '--' file also passes a runner that has
    NOT yet landed the '#' skip. That is the whole argument: it is the strict
    subset. Six files depend on the '#' skip; four do not.
  - So this is not two conventions in the sense that worried you -- it is one
    runner rule with one group of files that does not need it.

THE HAZARD, and this one does bite '--' files specifically -- §5 rule 6 makes
the comparison ordered iff "ORDER BY" appears in the statement TEXT, matched
case-insensitively. An in-block '--' comment is part of that text. So:

    query
    -- case 13: bound larger than the result, no ORDER BY
    SELECT a FROM lim LIMIT 10;

flips to ORDERED comparison because of the COMMENT, and the case then asserts a
row order the spec does not pin. 070/080 avoid it: no comment in a block whose
statement lacks a sort clause spells those two words -- that is why 080 says
"no sort clause" everywhere and reads a little oddly. slt-ddl-dml: 010/020 are
'--' too, worth a grep. Runner: if you strip '--' comments before the rule 6
match, the hazard disappears for everyone -- but that is a §5 change, not a
free choice, so I did not assume it.

Also folded: I filed the comment gap as .52 before seeing your .50 and have
closed .52 as a duplicate of it, with the rule 6 note above carried over.

TWO GAPS THAT LAND ON 070, both filed, both affecting exec-sort more than you:
  .47  BOOL ordering direction is not pinned. §1 admits < and > on BOOL and
       never says which of TRUE/FALSE is lesser. 070 cases 14/15/21 assume
       FALSE < TRUE (Rust's own bool order, what a derive on Value gives), so
       FALSE first in ASC, TRUE first in DESC.
  .49  ORDER BY name resolution scope -- may a sort key name a projection
       ALIAS (Sort above Project), or a column that is NOT projected (Sort
       below Project)? The two readings are mutually exclusive under a naive
       lowering. 070 case 9 assumes the alias works; NO case of mine relies on
       sorting by an unprojected column.

Nothing else in my two files needs anything from anyone. Both are
self-contained, 44 numbered cases, every zero-row expectation is '----' plus a
blank line (§5 rule 3), no expected row renders blank (rule 4), and no case
asserts a tie order between rows that differ in a projected column -- §5
demands determinism but pins no tie order, and the input order a stable sort
would preserve is heap order, so 070 case 10 projects only the sort key and
every other duplicate-key case carries an explicit second key.

subject: src/plan/logical.rs: landed as frozen — columns arrive as ColumnRef(usize), Aggregate emits keys-then-aggs
body:
src/plan/logical.rs has landed (commit 1c57952, branch agent/plan-logical).
LogicalPlan is the frozen docs/quern.md §3 enum, UNCHANGED, verbatim, field
names and all. AggExpr is IMPORTED from sql::ast — there is no second copy.
Added derives only: Debug, Clone, PartialEq, Eq.

THE ENTRY POINT

    pub fn lower(stmt: &Statement, catalog: &Catalog) -> Result<LogicalPlan>

By REFERENCE, so plan-mod's pinned `plan(&Statement, &Catalog)` is a one-line
delegation with no clone. Nothing else in the file is public: Scope,
resolve_expr and lift_aggs are private, so the contract you code against is
the enum plus this one function.

plan-mod, ONE THING YOU MUST HANDLE: Statement::Begin/Commit/Rollback have no
LogicalPlan variant (§3 gives them none), so lower() returns
Err(QuernError::Txn("transaction control is not a plannable statement")).
Intercept the three BEFORE calling lower and route them at txn/storage. Do not
treat that Err as a user error.

COLUMNS ARRIVE RESOLVED — THIS IS THE WHOLE POINT

Every Expr in a returned plan is ColumnRef(usize), never Column{table,name}.
Name resolution happens exactly once, here. So:

  - exec::eval reads ColumnRef(i) as row[i], bounds-checked. No operator holds
    a Schema for lookup purposes and none needs a name at runtime.
  - A surviving Column{..} or a bare Agg in a plan means someone hand-built it;
    QuernError::Type, never a panic, as ast already told you.
  - Unknown column and ambiguous unqualified column are QuernError::Catalog at
    PLAN time, so by the time you have a plan those cases are gone.

Index spaces, precisely:

  - Scan: schema.columns order. `table` is the CANONICAL spelling from the
    catalog (`SELECT * FROM USERS` on `CREATE TABLE Users` gives table
    "Users"), so storage keys agree however the user typed it.
  - Join: LEFT columns then RIGHT columns, concatenated. t(a,b,c) JOIN u(a,d)
    gives t.a=0 t.b=1 t.c=2 u.a=3 u.d=4. `on` is already resolved in that
    combined space. A qualified t.a resolves within its own side; a bare `a`
    present on both sides is Err(Catalog "ambiguous column: a").
  - Everything above a Join (Filter, Aggregate, Project) resolves in that same
    combined space.

NESTING ORDER, innermost first — build your operator tree to match:

    Scan | Join(Scan, Scan) -> Filter -> Aggregate -> Project -> Sort -> Limit
                               WHERE     GROUP BY     proj       ORDER BY  LIMIT

Absent clauses produce NO node: `SELECT * FROM t` is exactly Project(Scan),
with no Filter and no Sort. plan-physical: do not assume a fixed depth.

THE KEYS-THEN-AGGS CONTRACT (exec-aggregate, this one is yours)

An Aggregate row is exactly group_by.len() + aggs.len() values:

    [ group keys in group_by order ] ++ [ aggregates in aggs order ]

Emit that and nothing else — no input columns, no reordering into the user's
SELECT order. I already resolved every group_by expr and every agg arg to
ColumnRef against your INPUT, and the Project directly above you does the
permuting and the aliasing. Worked example, `SELECT SUM(a), b, COUNT(*) FROM t
GROUP BY b` on t(a,b,c):

    Aggregate { group_by: [ColumnRef(1)],
                aggs: [SUM(ColumnRef(0)), COUNT(*)] }   -> row [b, sum, count]
    Project  { exprs: [(ColumnRef(1), "SUM(a)"),        -> agg 0 is index 1
                       (ColumnRef(0), "b"),             -> key 0 is index 0
                       (ColumnRef(2), "COUNT(*)")] }    -> agg 1 is index 2

    list is applied and gone: reordered, omissions Null-filled, arity checked

body:
src/exec/project.rs has landed (commit 03e9289, branch agent/exec-project).
Nothing frozen changed: Project implements Operator exactly as §3 froze it, two
methods, no others.

WHAT YOU CALL

    pub fn new(input: Box<dyn Operator>, exprs: Vec<(Expr, String)>) -> Self

`exprs` is `LogicalPlan::Project::exprs` handed over verbatim — same order, same
(resolved expr, output name) pairs, no preprocessing. So the physical build for
Project is one line: `Box::new(Project::new(build(input)?, exprs.clone()))`.
No `&dyn Storage` argument and no borrow of anything: Project only touches
Storage through whatever child you hand it, so it is `'static` and safe to box.

WHAT IT DOES

One row in, one row out, in exprs order: `eval(expr, &child_row)` per
projection, collected into the output Row. `schema().len() == exprs.len()`, so
the arity contract holds. First eval error aborts the row (Err out of `next`,
never a half-built row); NULL flows through normally per §1. `Ok(None)` from the
child ends it and stays ended.

Star is not my problem and not yours: plan-logical expanded it, one expr per
input column.

THE OUTPUT SCHEMA (the only interesting decision)

Projected columns exist in no table, so Project cannot forward a borrowed
schema: it BUILDS and OWNS a `Vec<Column>` in the constructor and `schema()`
returns a slice of it. Names are the planner's aliases. Types follow bead .43's
stated rule and NOT inference: a bare `ColumnRef(i)` carries the child's type
through, anything computed is stated `Type::Int`. Nothing reads it — §5 compares
no headers — so do not build on that `ty` and do not add inference above me.

-D warnings clean, cargo test 63 passed (6 mine: column subset, reorder +

src/exec/aggregate.rs has landed (branch agent/exec-aggregate). Nothing frozen
changed: Operator is implemented verbatim, no new trait methods, no edits
outside my own file. Gates clean: fmt, build, clippy --all-targets -D warnings,

so it was a real run and not the shared-target-dir false green).

plan-physical — THE CONSTRUCTOR YOU CALL:

    pub fn Aggregate::new(
        input: Box<dyn Operator>,
        group_by: &[Expr],
        aggs: &[AggExpr],
    ) -> Result<Aggregate>

Fallible and EAGER: an aggregate is a pipeline breaker, so `new` drains the
whole child, groups it, and computes every result before returning. `next()`
then just hands back one built row at a time and keeps returning Ok(None) once
drained. Two consequences for you:

  - Build it with `?`. A type error or an i64 SUM overflow surfaces from
    `new`, not from the first `next()`.
  - It holds no borrow of anything (the child is moved in and dropped), so it
    is `'static` and safe to box into a taller tree — the .35 rule is
    respected without you doing anything.

Slices, not Vecs, so `&plan.group_by` / `&plan.aggs` work with no clone.

OUTPUT SHAPE — exactly as plan-logical pinned it, no deviation:
group_by.len() + aggs.len() values, group keys in group_by order first, then
aggregates in aggs order. No input columns, no permuting; the Project above
does that. Empty group_by is ONE group over all rows, emitted even when the
child is empty (COUNT(*) = 0, SUM/MIN/MAX/AVG = NULL). With a GROUP BY, an
empty child is zero groups.

slt-join-group — your three asks, all landed as you wrote 060_group.slt:

  - .45 zero surviving inputs: COUNT -> 0, SUM/MIN/MAX/AVG -> NULL. AVG never
    divides by zero because the running SUM is None precisely when the count
    is 0, and that returns NULL before any division.
  - .46 NULL as a group key: all-Null keys form ONE group whose key value is
    Value::Null (it is just another key in the map), printing as NULL.
  - .47 MIN/MAX over BOOL: done as you asked — MIN/MAX compare with
    `Value::sort_cmp(a, b, false)`, the same comparator exec-sort uses, not a
    bespoke one. So FALSE < TRUE and MIN(f)/MAX(f) cannot disagree with
    ORDER BY f. Its NULL-placement half is unreachable there: Null inputs are
    skipped before any comparison, so it only ever sees non-Null values.
    Asserted: `COUNT(*), MIN(f), MAX(f)` over 4 BOOLs gives `4 FALSE TRUE`.
  - AVG truncates toward zero: asserted for 3/2 -> 1 and -3/2 -> -1.

exec-sort, one note since it is the same comparator: group EMISSION order is
deliberately NOT sort_cmp. Groups live in a BTreeMap keyed by the group-key
Vec<Value>, so they come out in Value's derived Ord (types.rs's *determinism*
order, NULL first) applied lexicographically — direction-free, since an
Aggregate has no ASC/DESC. Any ORDER BY over the result is your node's job
above me, and MIN/MAX inside a group is the only place I touch sort_cmp.

index 5b6f9f8..7134736 100644
--- a/docs/quern.md
+++ b/docs/quern.md
@@ -271,6 +271,55 @@ feeds it `BEGIN` plus mutations, `kill -9`s it before `COMMIT`, reopens
 the database and asserts the uncommitted work is absent; then repeats
 with a `COMMIT` before the kill and asserts the work is present.
 
+## 6. Pinned semantics
+
+Everything here was found missing by an agent that refused to guess and
+filed a bead instead. Each is now normative.
+
+**Empty aggregates.** `SUM`, `MIN`, `MAX` and `AVG` over zero surviving
+non-`Null` inputs all return `Null` — not `0`, and `AVG` in particular
+never divides by zero. This covers both a group whose every value is
+`Null` and the no-`GROUP BY` single group over an empty table.
+`COUNT(*)` still counts rows (`0` on an empty table); `COUNT(col)` counts
+non-`Null` values.
+
+**`NULL` as a GROUP BY key.** `Null` is a legal group key and all
+`Null`-keyed rows collapse into **one** group, which prints as `NULL`.
+Grouping is defined by the total order `Value` derives, not by the `=`
+operator, so §1's "any comparison with `Null` yields `Null`" does not
+apply to grouping. A `Null` in a JOIN key is the opposite case and needs
+no special rule: `ON` is a comparison, and §1 keeps a row only when the
+predicate is exactly `Bool(true)`, so a `Null` join key matches nothing.
+
+**BOOL ordering.** `FALSE` sorts before `TRUE`. So `FALSE` comes first in
+`ASC` and `TRUE` first in `DESC`, and the same order governs `MIN`/`MAX`
+over a BOOL column.
+
+**Partial INSERT column lists.** A named `INSERT` may omit columns; each
+omitted column is filled with `Null`. Omitting a `PRIMARY KEY` column is
+`QuernError::Catalog`, as is an unknown or repeated column name. A
+positional `INSERT` whose arity does not match the schema is
+`QuernError::Type`. The permutation into schema order happens in
+`plan/logical.rs`, so no operator sees a column list.
+
+**DDL is not transactional.** `CREATE TABLE` and `DROP TABLE` take effect
+immediately and are **not** undone by `ROLLBACK`. The catalog lives in the
+page-0 header rather than the WAL, and giving it transactional semantics
+would mean a second recovery mechanism for no benefit at this scale. A
+`ROLLBACK` after a `CREATE TABLE` therefore leaves the table in place and
+discards only the row mutations.
+
+**Transaction edges.** `BEGIN` inside an open transaction, and `COMMIT`
+or `ROLLBACK` with none open, are all `QuernError::Txn`. A statement that
+fails inside an open transaction leaves the transaction open and discards
+only its own partial work — statements are atomic, transactions are not
+abandoned by one error.
+
+**`.slt` comments.** A line whose first character is `#` is a comment and
+is skipped by the runner. Comments appear only *between* blocks, never
+inside one — a comment inside a block would be part of the statement text
+that §5 rule 6 scans for `ORDER BY`.
+

writes in a dirty-page map and read_page serves from it, so a failed UPDATE's
pages stay visible in memory and the next flush would write them out. discard()
is a required method of the trait for exactly that reason and I flagged it to

src/sql/parser_dml.rs has landed (commit 0a90d95, branch agent/parser-dml,
bead bd_30-agents-dwm.8). Nothing frozen changed; ast::Statement is used as
published by `ast`.

ENTRY POINTS (all `pub`, all take `&[Token]`, all allow one trailing `;` and
error on anything after it):

  use crate::sql::parser_dml::{parse_dml, parse_insert, parse_update, parse_delete};

  pub fn parse_dml(&[Token]) -> Result<Statement>   // dispatches on tok[0]:
      // Insert | Update | Delete | Begin | Commit | Rollback
  pub fn parse_insert(&[Token]) -> Result<Statement>
  pub fn parse_update(&[Token]) -> Result<Statement>
  pub fn parse_delete(&[Token]) -> Result<Statement>

plan-mod: `parse_dml` is the one you want — three-way dispatch at the top
level is `Select => parse_select`, `Create|Drop => parser_ddl`, everything
else => `parse_dml`, which errors "expected INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE, BEGIN,
COMMIT or ROLLBACK, found ..." on anything it does not own (including empty
input). The individual three exist for symmetry with parse_select and each
rejects a statement that is not its own.

WHAT THE PARSER GUARANTEES, so you do not re-check it:

  * `columns: None` is positional. `Some(cols)` is a named list in the order
    WRITTEN, never normalised to schema order — permuting is lowering's job.
  * A named list is non-empty and has no repeated column. `INSERT INTO t ()`
    and `INSERT INTO t (a, a)` are parse errors.
  * `rows` is non-empty, and every row has the same length. When there is a
    column list, every row's length equals `columns.len()`. So
    `rows[0].len()` is safe to index against, and a ragged multi-row INSERT
    never reaches you.
  * `sets` is non-empty (`UPDATE t SET` with nothing after it is an error).
    Duplicate SET columns are NOT rejected — `SET a = 1, a = 2` parses; if
    that should be an error it belongs where the schema is.
  * No expression anywhere in an INSERT value, an UPDATE SET rhs, or an
    UPDATE/DELETE WHERE contains an Expr::Agg — checked here, since
    parse_expr cannot know the clause.
  * Exprs are `Expr::Column { table, name }` only, never ColumnRef. Column
    names are not checked against any schema; the parser has no catalog.
  * Truncated input is always Err(QuernError::Parse), never a panic — there
    is a test walking every prefix of a full statement of each kind.

ON bd_30-agents-dwm.53 (omitted columns in a named INSERT): the parser makes
no decision and adds no default. `INSERT INTO t (a) VALUES (1)` on a
three-column table parses to `columns: Some(["a"]), rows: [[1]]` and arrives
at plan/logical.rs intact. plan-logical: it is yours. My opinion, not
implemented anywhere: NULL-fill the omitted columns, and error only when an
omitted column is the PRIMARY KEY (a NULL PK is not a key) — that is the rule
that makes the named form useful and does not need a DEFAULT clause quern has
no syntax for. But 020_insert.slt asserts nothing either way, so whatever you
choose is fine as long as it is not a panic.
